The amount and uniformity of illuminance, and perhaps also light spectrum, are found to affect perceived personal safety (Boyce, 2000; Knight, 2009). Researchers have focused in particular on how sense of safety is influenced by features of the physical environment. Fisher and Nasar describe three such proximate cues: prospect, refuge, and escape (Fisher,1992). Street lighting is expected to affect peoples’ appraisal of prospect, and thus safety feelings (Haans, 2012). Adequate street lighting, for example, offers visibility, which is a prerequisite for prospect (Loewen, 1993). From a refuge perspective, street lighting can reduce these blind spots, but might also cast shadows in which potential offenders can hide (Nasar, 1997). As for escape, adequate street lighting might point street users to important possibilities for escape, and light emitting from windows might point to social activity, and thus support in case of an emergency. There was considerably more support for the premise that street lighting can have a role in reducing fear of crime than for the idea that street lighting can affect the occurrence of crime itself, reflecting the results of some studies (Herbert and Davidson, 1995; Vrij and Winkel, 1991). Pain found that not all of those who were fearful held this view, but, in general, those who were fearful felt most anxious at night (Pain, 2006). If there was more street lighting, most of 22 those who worried about crime said they would be less concerned. Reasons commonly given were that they “would feel able to see who’s around” and would have “more peace of mind.” However, some felt street lighting was fairly insignificant and improvements would not have an impact. Reasons given included beliefs about the causation of crime, as well as the fact that criminals were often known to be local: “it’s not just the lighting, it’s the people.” As some research has suggested, place and context appear highly significant to the relationship between street lighting, crime, and fear: lighting is most likely to ameliorate problems in stable, homogenous areas (Farrington and Welsh, 2002; Pease, 1999). In these study areas, residents’ caution appears to be well founded. The fact that most of the study areas were deprived areas in which community pride was described as decreasing rapidly by residents may be one reason for their doubt over whether street lighting would do much to improve safety (Pain, 2006). Pease (1999) speculates that, where street lighting does reduce crime and fear, the effect works through increased community pride and sense of ownership of the local area. While improved street lighting schemes are likely to have a range of other benefits, however, under different circumstances, a technical fix might be expected to have little effect, and should be part of wider social policies that also address the socioeconomic context of the area (Gilling, 1997). 2.2.3 Environment The impact of lighting on the environment is significant.
